subject: How to deal with large group size effect

messages.subject: How to deal with large group size effect
parts:
Dear All
If we have a species which is gregarious in nature ( Deer). The Cluster sizez varies from 1 to 200. Than Arithemetic mean ( which we use in distance sampling E (mean group size) is not the correct measure of central tendency as alternative I can use geometric mean of group size (E) X (DS= group density). Do we have any option in Distance to get this analysis done , where we can choose geomean for expected cluster size rather than arithmetic mean.??
regards:
Mayank

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
parts:
Variability in cluster size does not invalidate the arithmetic mean, nor justify use of the geometric mean.  However, size bias means that the arithmetic mean tends to be biased high.  (Larger groups are more likely to be detected, so the mean size of detected groups is larger than the mean size of all groups.)  The default method in Distance corrects for size bias.  Instead of the arithmetic mean, it uses regression of log cluster size on estimated probability of detection to predict mean cluster size when detection is certain (as there can be no size bias when all clusters are detected).  I can see no reason to prefer the geometric mean over this option.  If you really want to use the geometric mean, you can calculate it outside Distance, and include it as a multiplier in the analysis.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 9f336be8909c2db8
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
parts:
There is another aspect to group (cluster) size which we meet with in (low level, oblique) aerial census, namely counting bias. While a larger group is easier to detect than a smaller group (detection bias) a larger group is more difficult to count (counting bias). More animals are missed when counting larger groups than smaller groups, i.e. counting bias is positively associated with group size. We address this problem in aerial census in three ways: first, by using a fixed width of counting strip to minimise and hold constant detection bias, second by photographing groups >~10 to count later in the laboratory, and third by applying species/habitat group size correction factors. The fixed strip holds detection bias constant so we can concentrate on the big problem which is counting bias. Even so, we are still underestimating, especially with densely grouped species such as buffalo and livestock.

 

These subtle and difficult interactions between detection and counting bias may have an important effect on distance methods. For example, a group quite near to an observer and counted carefully many times to be 30 animals may well be "only" 32, while a group quite some way from the same observer and also counted equally carefully to be 30 animals may well be 36. Simply accounting for detection bias leaves counting bias unresolved.

 

We have recently been involved in an aerial census of Khulan and gazelle in 150,000 km2 of the Gobi desert, Mongolia,  (http://southgobi2013.countingstuff.org) using high resolution (2.5cm GSD) sample aerial photography (APS sampling). At exactly the same time a ground census using distance sampling overlapped in a 90,000km2 area. We have significant problems reconciling the two sets of census data. The output of the ground census seems worryingly sensitive to model parameterisation. In contrast, the aerial census database is built like a brick ----house and can take anything you can throw at it -- which is not the same as saying it is not "wrong"!

 

Best regards, Mike

 

Mike Norton-Griffiths

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] How to deal with large group size effect
parts:
Mike, yes, counting bias is a major problem.  With terrestrial or ship surveys, counting bias tends to be a function of distance from the line or point.  If you can assume no bias at zero distance, then the default regression method in the software Distance corrects for this bias as well as for detection bias.  However, in aerial surveys, that is unlikely to be the case, and the same is true of terrestrial surveys when groups flee from the observer before a good count can be made.

 

For aerial surveys, as technology improves, I expect observers to be replaced by high-resolution imagery surveys.  The aircraft can then fly higher, avoiding responsive movement.  Detectability tends not to fall off with distance, as the distance to the outer edge of the strip is much the same as directly below the aircraft (combination of high altitude and relatively narrow strip).  Data are available for validation, and correcting for mis-identifications and under-counting.  Availability remains an issue (e.g. diving animals for marine surveys, or animals hidden by canopy), but can be addressed.

 

If you have known-size groups, you can compare observer estimates with the known sizes, to estimate a correction.  E.g. for shipboard surveys, a helicopter taking photos of some of the groups might provide the known-sizes.  For terrestrial surveys, some groups might be watched from vantage points, while an observer is sent past.

 

Steve Buckland
